articles.title: GOP senators press Pentagon over Ukraine’s loss of Starshield data
articles.summary: Four Republican senators have joined their Democratic colleagues in pressing the Trump administration for information about whether Pentagon officials ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the satellite-based Starshield network, which Ukrainian officials said limited their ability to intercept Russian drones. Ukraine needs access to fast Starshield data speeds to operate drones along with fixed-wing and…
articles.body:
Four Republican senators have joined their Democratic colleagues in pressing the Trump administration for information about whether Pentagon officials ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the satellite-based Starshield network, which Ukrainian officials said limited their ability to intercept Russian drones.

Ukraine needs access to fast Starshield data speeds to operate drones along with fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft, which are critical to its national defense.

Ukraine’s full access to Starshield-provided data was quickly restored Wednesday, prompting speculation on Capitol Hill that President Trump didn’t make the call to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine but that the decision may have come from senior officials.

Four Republican senators — including two senior members of the Senate Intelligence Committee — signed a bipartisan letter to Platte Moring, the Pentagon’s inspector general, demanding he investigate whether any Department of Defense (DOD) or other U.S. government officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine.

Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, which provides internet connectivity from low-orbit satellites.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), a senior member of the Intelligence Committee, signed the letter, along with Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), another member of the Intelligence panel, and Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Thom Tillis (N.C.).

The GOP lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over reports that Ukraine lost access to high-speed internet connectivity enabling them to operate military vehicles flying faster than 63 mph or faster than 100 mph, hampering their ability to fend off Russian strikes.

“We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances,” the senators wrote.

Tillis is not running for reelection, while Cornyn lost a primary after the president backed his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Collins is in a tough reelection race in a state Trump has lost in three consecutive presidential elections, while Murkowski is known for breaking with the president on various issues.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, spearheaded the letter.

Democratic Sens. Dick Durbin (Ill.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Chris Coons (Del.) and Jack Reed (R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, also signed it.

A Senate source familiar with internal discussions about how to respond to Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to critical military intelligence said senators in both parties have questions about whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or other senior defense officials — such as Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy — were involved in the decision.

Lawmakers blamed Hegseth and Colby, the No. 3-ranking Pentagon official, last year for repeatedly holding up shipments of missiles and ammunition to Ukraine.

Tillis, a leading advocate of U.S. military support for Ukraine, first called on the Pentagon’s inspector general Wednesday evening to investigate the matter.

He expressed skepticism that Hegseth would answer senators’ questions about the Starshield outage if called to testify on Capitol Hill.

“The latest reporting suggests this strategic snafu may have occurred more locally within DOD Starshield systems, not with Starlink or SpaceX,” Tillis wrote on social media Wednesday.

“I’m not holding my breath for Defense Secretary Hegseth to offer transparency, so we’ll be asking the DOD Inspector General to initiate an investigation and report back to Congress and the American People,” he said.

“At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscience [conscious] decision to clear the field for a Russian attack,” Tillis fumed.

John Ullyot, a former spokesperson for the Senate Armed Services Committee and former deputy assistant to Trump, said senators have good reason to question senior Pentagon officials for answers about the Starshield outage.

“Hegseth reportedly cut off weapons to Ukraine without the President’s sign-off three times in his first six months on the job, so it’s not surprising senators want to know if he was involved here as well,” Ullyot said.

“Either way, Republicans shouldn’t have to be dealing with these distractions from DoD less than three weeks before the midterms,” he added.

Senators who support continued U.S. military aid to Ukraine believe Hegseth’s office ordered a temporary halt to military aid flights to Ukraine in early February 2025 without notifying the White House.

The halt to air traffic reportedly impacted nearly a dozen shipments of artillery shells and weapons from Dover Air Force Base and a base in the United Arab Emirates.

Hegseth was accused of unilaterally delaying military aid to Ukraine again in May and July of last year.

The Pentagon said in July 2025 that it delayed weapons shipments to Ukraine because of a concern over low stockpiles, but lawmakers at the time rejected that rationale.

Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, at the time argued that the Pentagon’s stockpile of weapons and ammunition wasn’t any lower than it had been in the previous three and a half years of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Republican national security insiders think that if senior DOD officials ordered a limitation on Ukraine’s access to Starshield and other critical intelligence sharing, they may have acted without Trump’s explicit knowledge or approval.

Suspicion on Capitol Hill over whether Hegseth, Colby or other senior Pentagon officials played a role in limiting Ukraine’s access to Starshield gained momentum Wednesday after Elon Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, which owns and operates Starlink, pointed the finger at the Pentagon.

Musk wrote on X, the social media platform which he also owns, that “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately” the president of the United States.

Ukraine’s access to Starshield was quickly restored after the disruptions to high-speed data attracted media scrutiny and criticism from Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday called the loss of access to Starshield a “big mistake.”

“People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful,” he warned.

articles.title: Former Border Patrol chief recalls Biden migrant surge chaos as Trump crackdown delivers historic turnaround
articles.summary: As DHS announces lowest fiscal year border crossings in American history, retired Yuma Sector Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem recalls agents being outnumbered 100 to 1, and warns the historic lows could face new threats.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s border crackdown has sharply reduced the illegal crossings that overwhelmed agents under former President Joe Biden, with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reporting Thursday historic lows in apprehensions and a full fiscal year without Border Patrol releasing migrants into the country. For retired Yuma Arizona Sector U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem, the turnaround stands in sharp contrast to days when his agents could not pick up migrants fast enough and the consequences spilled into neighborhoods, farms and local businesses. "They just started walking through the agriculture fields. They started running through town," Clem told Fox News Digital, recalling the surge in December 2021. "They started going to the food bank. They started knocking on people’s doors at all hours of the nights." TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% But while Clem said he credits stronger enforcement and the prospect of deportation with helping drive the decline, he warned that the gains could face another threat — a political shift in Washington. "There are a lot of policy decisions that can be really jammed up by a Congress that’s gung-ho to overturn what this president has done," said Clem, who warned that changes in congressional control could complicate enforcement through funding decisions and policy restrictions, while a future presidential administration could pursue broader reversals. Preliminary DHS figures released Thursday show Border Patrol recorded 98,708 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026, roughly 95% below the annual average of more than 1.8 million during the Biden administration. That translates to about 270 apprehensions a day across the southwest border, compared with roughly 5,000 using the department’s Biden-era annual average. In Yuma alone, Clem recalled daily arrivals climbing from roughly 25 in December 2020, to more than 1,000 by December 2021. During a particularly difficult three-day stretch that month, he said, daily arrivals approached 1,500. TRUMP HITS DRAMATIC MILESTONE IN MASSIVE DEPARTURE FROM BIDEN BORDER PLAN: 'WHAT A DIFFERENCE' Weather problems and a shortage of resources compounded the strain, leaving agents struggling to transport people from the border, he said. "That was really when it, you know, was the most critical for me because we had the true community impact of a failed border security policy out of Washington, D.C.," Clem said. His agents remained committed to the mission, he said, but the volume was overwhelming. "The agents, their heads were in the right place. They knew they had to do the job," Clem said. "But when you’re outnumbered, literally 100 to one, it’s very difficult." The new DHS figures put an entire fiscal year of southwest border apprehensions below half the 249,740 recorded during the Biden administration’s single busiest month. DHS also said September marked the 17th consecutive month without Border Patrol releasing migrants into the country, completing what it described as the agency’s first full fiscal year with zero releases. DHS TOUTS MILLIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DEPARTURES AS BORDER CROSSINGS DROP 94% UNDER TRUMP Clem said the prospect of being released had given smugglers a powerful selling point during the previous administration. "If you get to the border, you’re gonna be processed, and you’ll be let go," he said, describing the pitch. He argued that changing that expectation is central to discouraging illegal crossings. "They know that they’re not gonna be processed and released, which was the status quo under the Biden-Harris administration," Clem said. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY He credited a combination of personnel, infrastructure, technology and consequences for illegal entry, rather than any single measure. The enforcement effort also extends beyond the border itself. Clem said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations inside the country add another layer, making clear that getting past Border Patrol does not eliminate the possibility of arrest and removal. "When you combine the strong border posture, as well as the strong and robust interior enforcement, it’s a recipe for success," he said. Border czar Tom Homan pointed to that interior enforcement push Thursday, saying ICE had recorded its highest single-day deportation total since Trump returned to office. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER "We are deportation-maxxing—firing on all cylinders while still expanding our capabilities to ramp up removals beyond current record-breaking levels," Homan wrote on social media. Homan said he visited ICE Air Operations in Alexandria, Louisiana, to observe removal operations, including a flight returning Haitians he said had criminal records involving aggravated assault, sexual assault, kidnapping, battery and other offenses. He also said ICE conducted more removals in September than in any other month, though his post did not provide totals or specify the comparison period. Fiscal year 2026 figures were still being finalized, he said. The ICE removal figures measure a separate part of the immigration system from Border Patrol apprehensions and releases. "President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement announcing the border figures. "The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works." Still, Clem cautioned that lower numbers do not eliminate threats from smugglers or people trying to evade detection. "There are always gonna be that risk where somebody does sneak through. Who is that person?" he said. He argued that mixed political messages can also give smugglers an opening to lure people into dangerous journeys with promises that U.S. policies will change. "When our policies aren’t clear and transparent, and we’re not holding ourselves accountable, it’s a marketing tool for the smuggling organizations," he said. For Clem, the distinction between debating immigration policy and maintaining border security is essential. "We need to find a way to retain and recruit those that are here, that are foreign nationals that want to contribute." "But none of that should matter when it comes down to securing the border," Clem added. "We should always be looking at keeping America safe."

articles.title: Are clocks falling back this weekend? Here's what to know
articles.summary: The annual clock change is still on. Here's when daylight saving time ends and why Americans will "fall back" on hour.
articles.body:
Americans will turn their clocks back one hour on Nov. 1 after Congress adjourned without passing legislation that would end the nation's twice-yearly time change.

Despite pressure from President Donald Trump and growing public support for ending clock changes, lawmakers have yet to send the Sunshine Protection Act to the president's desk.

For now, federal law remains unchanged, and most Americans should prepare to turn their clocks back one hour on Nov. 1.

Here's what you need to know about daylight saving time.

When does daylight saving time end in 2026?

Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1, when clocks move back one hour to 1 a.m.

The change marks the return to standard time and gives Americans an extra hour of sleep. It also brings earlier sunsets and more morning daylight as winter approaches.

Under current law, daylight saving time begins on the second Sunday in March and ends on the first Sunday in November.

Why are Americans still changing their clocks?

The answer is simple: Congress has not yet changed the law.

The Sunshine Protection Act , which would make daylight saving time permanent and eliminate the twice-yearly clock changes, passed the House in July by a 301-117 vote. But the legislation has stalled in the Senate, the final hurdle before it could reach Trump's desk.

Lawmakers left Washington before taking up the measure, leaving the existing system intact.

As a result, clocks across most of the country remain on track to fall back Nov. 1.

Trump has repeatedly urged Congress to end the twice-yearly clock change and keep the nation on daylight saving time year-round.

"Republicans in the Senate have to get moving on what I call the ' No More Changing of Clocks Act ,' officially known as The Sunshine Protection Act," Trump wrote in an Oct. 2 post on Truth Social.

Calling the current system "ridiculous," Trump argued that changing clocks twice a year is costly, stressful and unpopular with the public.

"People don't want to go around changing their Clocks anymore and, besides, far and away, most people like having an hour of extra sunlight in the evening, rather than in the morning," he added.

Everything he said: Trump on daylight saving time

Are Republican lawmakers split on permanent daylight saving time?

Despite Trump's support, several Senate Republicans remain unconvinced.

Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas has said that while he dislikes changing clocks, Congress previously experimented with permanent daylight saving time only to reverse course after many Americans objected to extremely late winter sunrises.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune has also expressed skepticism, telling Politico on Oct. 5 that there is " no clear path forward " for legislation to make daylight saving time permanent.

Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi raised similar concerns, citing safety issues in northern and rural states where children could be waiting for school buses in darkness during winter mornings.

That opposition has become a significant obstacle for legislation that appeared to have momentum earlier this year.

Polls suggest many Americans support ending the practice.

A 2023 YouGov survey found 62% of Americans favored ending the time changes. A January 2025 Gallup poll similarly found that 54% wanted to eliminate the practice.

Yet Americans remain divided on what should replace it.

Some support permanent daylight saving time, which would provide more daylight in the evening. Others favor permanent standard time, which would bring more morning sunlight during winter months.

The debate gained additional attention in March 2025 when Elon Musk , then leading Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, conducted a poll on X asking users whether they preferred clocks staying an hour earlier or later if the changes were eliminated.

More than 1.3 million users responded, with 58% favoring later daylight and 42% preferring earlier daylight.

Is permanent daylight saving time actually a good idea?

While many Americans agree they dislike changing clocks twice a year, experts remain divided on whether permanent daylight saving time is the answer.

Sleep researchers generally agree that switching clocks can disrupt circadian rhythms and affect sleep. But many experts argue that permanent standard time would be healthier than permanent daylight saving time because it aligns more closely with the body's natural clock.

Christopher Barnes , a professor at the University of Washington's Foster School of Business, said daylight saving time's appeal often comes from the promise of brighter evenings.

"A lot of people seem to like daylight saving time because there is more daylight available in the evening, and they envision themselves having many evening barbecues outside that they may enjoy," Barnes told USA TODAY.

But he warned that permanent daylight saving time could create long-term circadian misalignment for many Americans.

"The high prevalence of permanent circadian misalignment that permanent daylight savings time would produce would be bad for sleep and health outcomes," Barnes said, adding that sleep disruptions are linked to lower workplace engagement, reduced performance, diminished creativity and other negative effects.

Do all states observe daylight saving time?

Several states and U.S. territories remain on standard time year-round :

Most of Arizona (except the Navajo Nation)

How did daylight saving time become law?

The Uniform Time Act of 1966 , signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson, established the framework for daylight saving time in the United States.

Only Congress can permanently change the nation's twice-yearly clock-changing system, though the U.S. secretary of transportation oversees its administration under federal law.

For now, neither has changed the current system.

Whether lawmakers ultimately choose permanent daylight saving time, permanent standard time or leave the current system unchanged, Americans are still set for one more clock change this year. Unless Congress acts, clocks across most of the country will fall back one hour at 2 a.m. on Nov. 1.

Contributing: Reuters; Bart Jensen, Zachary Schermele, Jorge L. Ortiz, Fernando Cervantes Jr., Emily DeLetter, Julia Gomez, Kinsey Crowley, USA TODAY

Saman Shafiq is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at sshafiq@usatodayco.com and follow her on X and Instagram @saman_shafiq7.

articles.title: ‘President Bezos’ — primed to save America in 2028?
articles.summary: An opinion piece explores whether Jeff Bezos might pursue the presidency in 2028, weighing his massive wealth and technological expertise against potential conflicts of interest involving current President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
In early 2023, prominent Democrats were antsy about President Biden’s 2024 reelection prospects. A movement emerged to recruit primary challengers.

Prompted by a Hill op-ed advocating for a “superstar” to block then-former President Trump from being reelected, I proposed that Jeff Bezos could “make America Amazon .” “In these perilous times,” I wrote, “Bezos’s skills are needed. New technologies, artificial intelligence, and cyber warfare will rule the world, and China threatens.”

Over three years later, those technologies are spinning out of control, threatening a science-fiction scenario in which “AI could kill all humans.” Most worrisome is U.S. leaders’ inability to understand, legislate, regulate, and manage these fast-evolving, complex technological innovations. Americans are now helplessly watching a Ferrari race a 1908 Ford Model T.

Thus, on Oct. 5, I was fascinated to see a “President Bezos?” headline in the Drudge Report, linked to a Substack exclusive by Rob Shuter. He quoted unnamed sources, which suggests the story was either bunk or a well-placed strategic trial balloon, amplified by Drudge’s well-trafficked site .

Shuter’s sources said that Jeff Bezos’s wife, Lauren Sanchez Bezos, “loves the idea of President Bezos.” After attending the White House state dinner for China’s President Xi Jinping, “Lauren has become increasingly fascinated by Washington.” According to the source, “Lauren looks at Jeff and sees someone who conquered business, built a space company and became one of the most powerful men alive.” That leaves Mrs. Bezos asking, “What’s left?” because “in her mind the presidency is the ultimate final act.”

I would warn against underestimating Lauren Bezos’s drive and influence. In record time, she transformed her once-geeky-looking boyfriend, now husband, into an A-list celebrity. With hundreds of billions of dollars, nothing is impossible.

According to Forbes’ daily tracking of billionaires’ wealth, Jeff Bezos is, at this writing, the world’s second-richest man, worth $373 billion. That is far behind Elon Musk at $914 billion, but Bezos could yet catch up. Perhaps Mrs. Bezos won’t be satisfied until her husband is both the richest and most powerful man alive, not “one of” the most powerful, which explains why the “ultimate final act” is so appealing.

Surely, Bezos has the intellect, management skills, and gravitas to be president, and recent history shows that prior elected office isn’t required. Therefore, one could argue that because managing, taming, and utilizing technology is key to 21st-century national growth, global leadership, and political/economic survival, Bezos should run for president. Moreover, during a recent Fox News interview, Bezos revealed what could be construed as his futuristic policy platform.

A Bezos presidential campaign would start with high national name-recognition; not all of it is positive, but presidential campaigns are about branding yourself for the moment.

Most Americans already have a relationship with Bezos already, through the companies he personally owns and the corporations that Amazon owns . Bezos founded Amazon and still owns roughly 8 percent of it , making him the largest single shareholder with 879 million shares.

Amazon’s cash cow is Amazon Web Services , a cloud computing internet platform and AI behemoth making billions with corporate and federal contracts . It partners with the government — in fact, it is practically an arm of the government.

Let’s say Mrs. Bezos convinced her husband to enter a presidential primary; he wouldn’t need to fundraise. Bezos could easily spend $5 billion on his primary and general campaigns with no financial repercussions. Supporters could attend no-cost “Make America Amazon” receptions.

Amazon’s movie studios could produce his political ads — after all, Trump has normalized the blurring of lines between business and political interests. Amazon could sell “Bezos 2028” branded campaign merch, including watches, Bibles and sneakers , because Trump has set a precedent.

However, presidential candidate Bezos would face a perilous obstacle. In 2023, I assumed he would run as a Democrat . But now he wholeheartedly engages in Trump’s pay-to-play game , supporting the president’s vanity projects and the first lady’s movie . But if Bezos ran as a Republican and criticized Trump’s policies, he would risk losing untold billions in AWS government contracts and, for Blue Origin , Bezos’s space-travel company, his true passion.

He is already familiar with the consequences of Trump’s wrath. In 2019, Bezos lost a $10 billion Pentagon contract for AWS , allegedly because of Trump’s personal vendetta over negative reporting at the Bezos-owned Washington Post.

If Bezos were to run as a Democrat, the financial repercussions could be even greater, creating a no-win situation. Until Trump leaves office on Jan. 20, 2029, he will closely monitor who is with him and who is against him.

The consolation prize for rejecting a presidential run is that Bezos remains very powerful from outside the White House since money equals power. And his new corollary, “success is not villainy,” sums up the billionaire tech-bro era.

Still, if he wants it, and if Mrs. Bezos is interested in running for first lady, their campaign slogan could be, “It’s Prime Time in America!”

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill .

articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Sherrod Brown's pledge turns advice and consent into a punchline
articles.summary: Ohio's Sherrod Brown pledged to vote against every Trump judicial nominee regardless of qualifications, abandoning Senate advice and consent duties.
articles.body: In Ohio, Sherrod Brown went full Jaime West this week in his U.S. Senate campaign. West is the Indiana candidate who became a viral sensation for pledging to "fire all Republicans" because "I just don't like them." Brown appears to be eager to jump on the same rage train and pledged that he will vote against any Republican judicial nominee regardless of their qualifications or background. Brown is literally pledging that he will toss away the constitutional duty of "advice and consent" under Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution and vote blindly against anyone nominated by President Trump because he does not like him. Brown told MS NOW that "we’re not, obviously, confirming judges that are Trump judges." Unfortunately, it is common for senators of the opposing party to vote against a president's nominees. However, they at least preserve the pretense of "advice and consent." Brown is trying to win the race to the bottom by saying that Trump could nominate Louis Brandeis, and he would still vote against him because he is a Trump judicial nominee. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS Brown seems to be channeling Jaime West, who admitted that she does "not even talk to them" and hates Republicans. It is a curious pledge in a state that voted for Trump three times and is Republican. What is most concerning is that this pledge is made as leading Democrats are lining up in favor of packing the Court. The combination would ravage our court system through packing and attrition. Brown would simply not confirm any new judges as a way of reducing Republican judges on the bench. Brown and his colleagues are given absolute discretion in casting their votes on judicial nominees, including doing so on a strictly partisan basis. They also have the right not to vote on a nominee, as was the case of the nomination of Merrick Garland. While I also criticized the failure to vote on Garland, it was within the authority of the Senate to forego such a vote. There was a time when the Senate was called the "world’s greatest deliberative body." The phrase attributed to former President James Buchanan in 1867 is often repeated today like a mantra by senators who have dispensed with serious deliberations in favor of endless demonstrations. Now, Brown is actually running on a "no deliberation" pledge. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE I am old enough to remember when senators routinely voted for judges from the other party and different ideologies as a matter of political integrity. For many decades, senators insisted that they were bound to vote for a nominee if they were qualified even if they disagreed with their liberal or conservative jurisprudential views. In his famous 1878 "Kin Beyond the Sea," British Prime Minister William Gladstone referred to the U.S. Senate as "that remarkable body, the most remarkable of all the inventions of modern politics, the Senate of the United States." With Brown, even the pretense of deliberation is over. He is pledging not to consider the merits of nominees in fulfilling his oath to give "advice and consent" on nominations. Joining Jaime West, he is announcing that he just does not like them, and so he will not speak with them. The senators now seem to be offering pure undiluted rage to voters. In Rage and the Republic, I discuss how the Framers designed our Constitution to prevent a democracy from becoming what Benjamin Rush called a mobocracy. It is now becoming the captive of the very blind passions that it was designed to resist. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Brown pledge is a chilling moment for this once august institution. It was designed to be a bulwark against the mob, an institution that would temper passions, not yield to them. Indeed, in his final farewell to the Senate in 1805, Aaron Burr remarked that "if the Constitution be destined ever to perish by the sacrilegious hand of the demagogue or the usurper, which God avert, its expiring agonies will be witnessed on this floor."

articles.title: Vance and Ocasio-Cortez face off in Michigan, previewing possible 2028 match-up

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Vice President Vance are lending their star power to frontline candidates in Michigan, offering an early glimpse into what could be a potential…
articles.body:
▪ Zacharia confirms she didn’t pass bar exam

▪ Elections offices receive suspicious letters

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Vice President Vance are lending their star power to frontline candidates in Michigan, offering an early glimpse into what could be a potential 2028 presidential match-up.

Both parties see Michigan as essential to securing control of the Senate. No Republican has won a Senate race in Michigan since 1994, but the GOP sees retiring Sen. Gary Peters ‘s (D) seat as perhaps their best pickup opportunity this cycle. If Democrats lose it, they would need to pick up another five seats held by Republicans to win a majority.

Ocasio-Cortez appeared with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s conservative Upper Peninsula yesterday, bringing their “It Shouldn’t Be This Hard” bus tour to Escanaba, Iron Mountain and Marquette.

El-Sayed focused primarily on cost-of-living issues as he sought to court more right-leaning voters, telling hundreds of supporters they should reach out to people in their lives who support President Trump , saying, “They’re paying $5 gas, too.”

The Democratic duo could not escape questions about 2028 ambitions, however. At a campaign stop at a ski lodge in Iron Mountain, Mich., a 9-year-old asked whether they were going to become president or vice president.

“Here’s what I’m interested in doing: I’m interested in being your next United States senator,” El-Sayed said, stepping in to answer the question. When he said he hoped the young questioner could be an intern for him during his second term, Ocasio-Cortez laughed and clapped, The New York Times reported .

The congresswoman has said she will make a decision about her future plans after the midterms, acknowledging in a Times interview last month that some say she has “ a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot.”

Ocasio-Cortez will part from El-Sayed today as she heads out for solo campaign stops in southeast Michigan, appearing with Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) at an Oakland County Students for Abdul rally in Pontiac, before they are joined by Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) for a Henry Ford College rally in Dearborn. In the evening, Ocasio-Cortez will host a Latinos for Abdul rally in Detroit.

Meanwhile, Vance — who is hoping to secure his place as Trump’s heir apparent — stumped for several GOP candidates at an event yesterday in Monroe, Mich., where attendees were lining up hours before he was slated to speak.

The vice president called the Senate contest “the most important race in the United States of America” as he drew a contrast between Republican nominee Mike Rogers , a former House member, and El-Sayed, a former public health official.

“Normal people in this nation have watched the far left rally around causes that were fundamentally about destroying our foundations, destroying our basic identity as a nation,” Vance said at the rally. “They would say things, and then enact them, like ‘defund the police.’ They would say, ‘No one is illegal on stolen land.’ They would say, ‘We must abolish whiteness.’”

Trump, who will rally for Rogers in Michigan later this month, has also attacked El-Sayed for his immigrant background. During remarks at a Rose Garden luncheon yesterday, the president said El-Sayed “is a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100 percent.”

El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents, has denied any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which the U.S. earlier this year designated a terrorist organization. The issue resurfaced in recent days after news reports dug up old social media posts from El-Sayed’s half-sister that referenced their mother and her “activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the 70s.”

“I have no ties. We have no ties. I have never had these conversations with my mother. I wasn’t raised by my mother,” El-Sayed told NBC in an interview this week when asked about the issue. “ You’re using hearsay evidence from a tweet. It’s just not serious.”

If Democrats do win the Senate majority, as they are slightly favored to do, the next question would be what their agenda looks like in the chamber with divided government back in place.

The Hill’s Helen Huiskes has a rundown of Senate Democrats’ top priorities if they retake the majority. Insiders can click here to read more.

▪ The Hill : Susan Collins , Troy Jackson joust in final Senate debate.

Three students and one teacher were killed following a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., after a 16-year-old male opened fire with a long gun, the city’s police chief said. The suspect was also killed.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in an interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity on Thursday night. Earlier in the day, she said she had already been registered to take it before planning a move to China and knew the results would be “somewhat inconsequential.”

Ukraine resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries Thursday despite President Trump urging both sides to accept an energy ceasefire. The move comes at a difficult time for Ukraine, as it has been cut off from access to Elon Musk’s Starlink and reportedly run out of U.S.-made Patriot air defense missiles .

President Trump talks with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after a roundtable on criminal cartels in the State Dining Room of the White House, Oct. 23, 2025, in Washington. (Evan Vucci, Associated Press file)

DON SAYS NO : Trump showed the limits of what he will allow from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday when he announced that the military execution of the Fort Hood shooter will not be livestreamed as the Pentagon chief had planned.

The president announced on social media that he was canceling the livestream execution of Nidal Malik Hasan , who carried out the 2009 attack at the Texas military base that claimed 13 lives. Another 32 people were injured in the shooting.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Hegseth had announced the livestream for the scheduled Dec. 3 execution earlier this month, but the proposal received bipartisan backlash as critics compared it to the actions of terrorists and authoritarian regimes.

The president’s announcement marks a rare instance of Trump publicly blocking one of Hegseth’s moves. The Pentagon chief has overseen several controversial moves during his tenure, including a major overhaul the Defense Department’s top ranks.

▪ The Hill : Five takeaways as Trump shuts down Pentagon plan.

▪ The Hill : 80 percent in poll opposed livestreamed execution.

OMAR PROBE : Federal authorities have seized Rep. Ilhan Omar ’s (D-Minn.) phone and personal computers as part of their investigation reportedly concerning alleged fraud involving her immigration paperwork.

The New York Times reported that Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor , and at least one other family member have also received subpoenas as part of the federal grand jury probe.

Investigators are looking into whether Omar may be older than the date listed on her immigration paperwork, which would mean she would have needed to apply for citizenship by herself as an adult rather than through her father as a minor, according to The Wall Street Journal .

Omar’s office maintained that the investigation is based on lies.

▪ The Hill : Kristi Noem ‘confident’ Omar will ‘be held accountable.’

▪ The Hill : Marjorie Taylor Greene labels investigation as ‘bulls—.’

ON GUARD : Election offices nationwide are on alert after officials in three states reported suspicious packages were sent to them in the past week.

The top elections officials in Ohio, Oklahoma and Louisiana all confirmed an envelope containing a white powdery substance was mailed to them. In Ohio, the U.S. Postal Service blocked the delivery of the letter, while offices were evacuated in Oklahoma and Louisiana.

Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said law enforcement found “no evidence of harmful substances” after running tests.

The FBI told The Hill that the agency and Postal Service were investigating suspicious mailings nationally, including at secretary of State and election offices.

▪ Roll Call : Suspicious packages target senators on anniversary of attack.

FOLLOWING UP : The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic as part of the agency’s federal probe into the potential risks the firms’ AI models pose to the public.

Several high-profile cybersecurity incidents concerning the AI agents have added to public scrutiny about their safety recently. Earlier this year, OpenAI’s agents escaped during a test and hacked the tech startup Hugging Face.

More recently, Anthropic revealed that one of its models submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department in July.

The leaders of various AI companies have called for more guardrails to slow down AI development. They signed a pledge laying out voluntary commitments for developing the technology late last month.

▪ The Hill : Anthropic’s PAC spent more than $250,000 in third quarter.

IN THE WATER : Senate Democrats are demanding answers over an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) study to detect the abortion pill mifepristone in drinking water.

Every member of the Senate Democratic Caucus signed a letter Thursday to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, urging him to remove mifepristone and misoprostol from the list of emerging contaminants targeted for surveillance. They also pressed for specifics about the review.

Searching for traces of the two drugs in drinking water has been a focus of lobbying from anti-abortion activists for years. The Hill’s Nathaniel Weixel reports that there’s no evidence that abortion pills are harming the water supply or are harmful to people.

Medication abortion has become the most common method of abortion, particularly since the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022.

▪ The New York Times : Anti-abortion activists being sued under abortion pill law.

▪ The Hill : MAHA group spends big on Iowa governor’s race.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 10 a.m. He will travel to Dalton, Ga., where he will deliver remarks at 2:45 p.m., and then travel to Palm Beach, Fla., for a Republican National Committee event at 7:30 p.m.

The Supreme Court is pictured on Oct. 5, 2026, in Washington. (Mariam Zuhaib, Associated Press)

CHECKS AND BALANCES : The Trump administration is seeking to break new ground in its moves to limit judges’ authority to block the president’s agenda.

The Department of Justice asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to declare that judges can’t set aside federal agency rules nationwide when they find them unlawful. If the court gave a green light, that would add another victory for the administration after it curtailed judges’ ability to issue nationwide injunctions last year.

But The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports that this would be a steeper climb.

Former President Biden ’s administration tried advancing this argument, but Chief Justice John Roberts pushed back on it as “fairly radical,” while Justice Brett Kavanaugh called it “far-reaching.”

The three other conservative justices expressed some sympathy for the argument.

The legal fight concerns the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs lawsuits challenging the regulations from across the federal government. It directs judges to “hold unlawful and set aside agency action” they find to be “arbitrary, capricious,” unconstitutional or exceeding an agency’s power.

Judges have interpreted that to mean that they can block actions nationwide, and it’s been a regular tool in lawsuits concerning the most consequential presidential actions.

It’s been the ire of presidents of both parties. But the path to overturning it may be difficult.

▪ The Hill : Appeals court revives suits against transgender policy threats.

A person walks past ice covered trees Jan. 28, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. (George Walker IV, Associated Press)

WINTER OUTLOOK : The latest seasonal forecast from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center shows a split picture of what the country should expect for the end of fall and early winter.

The forecast released Thursday shows the broad weather patterns that states should expect in the final two months of this year and first month of next year. The projections are in line with what’s expected from the El Niño weather pattern that has had wide implications for the climate throughout the year.

In the coming months, states in the northern half of the country are most likely to see above-average warmth between November and January. That includes the Pacific Northwest, the Midwest through the Ohio Valley and into New England.

Other states in the south aren’t necessarily expected to be colder than usual, but the forecast is less clear, and they have an equal chance of being abnormally warm or cold or having a normal winter season.

The forecast for precipitation is the opposite, with many of the states most likely to be warmer also more likely to be dry. An area toward the south from California all the way to Florida and up the eastern coast is leaning toward above-average rain.

The forecast comes as a super El Niño appears increasingly likely .

articles.title: Alaska Senate candidates clash over the Iran war, high prices and their times in office
articles.summary: The two major candidates vying for an Alaska Senate seat squared off Thursday night over issues ranging from the war with Iran to controversies during the Democratic nominee’s time in Congress in a debate that at times flared into personal attacks.
articles.body: The two major candidates vying for an Alaska Senate seat squared off Thursday night over issues ranging from the war with Iran to controversies during the Democratic nominee’s time in Congress in a debate that at times flared into personal attacks. Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan described Democratic challenger Mary Peltola as someone who sought a lobbying paycheck after her time serving in the House ended in 2025, pointing to recent reporting on the tumult in her congressional office during her tenure. Peltola sought to tie Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran to the increase in the cost of living at home, pointing out Sullivan’s own increase in wealth while in office. The race between Sullivan and Peltola, which NBC News rates as a toss-up, is one of a handful that could determine control of the Senate in November. Democrats have targeted the seat as one of five potential pickup opportunities, despite the fact that Donald Trump carried Alaska by double digits in 2024. When asked what he thought of the White House’s recent announcement that it would allow the release of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market, Sullivan drew a distinction between himself and the Trump administration, a tack other Republicans in tight races have taken in recent debates. “I just led the effort on a Russia sanctions act that passed the Congress, so I’m opposed to that,” Sullivan said. The senator then pivoted to his opposition to the Pentagon’s now withdrawn announcement that it would livestream the execution of convicted terrorist Nidal Hasan. “Certainly he needs to be executed, but if you have a livestreaming of this terrorist, you are going to create more terrorists,” Sullivan said. Asked about the war with Iran, both candidates said the conflict should end soon. Peltola attributed the increase in prices at home to the ongoing conflict — issues that polling has shown have become a drag on Republicans heading into the midterms. “There does not appear to be a peace deal on the horizon, and I think it’s so important that our military be removed and protected,” Peltola said when asked whether she would support ending the war without a peace deal. Sullivan said he supported President Donald Trump’s war powers in Iran because “the largest state sponsor of terrorism should not have nuclear weapons.” “But it needs to end soon. The energy costs from this war are too high,” Sullivan continued, adding that boosting domestic energy production would bring down costs. In another exchange, Sullivan leveled criticism of Peltola’s lobbying work after losing her the state’s at-large House seat in 2024. “Mary, you’re walking through the revolving door so much you must be getting dizzy up here,” Sullivan said. Peltola responded by noting the increase in Sullivan’s net worth during his two terms as a senator. “Dan’s been in D.C. for 12 years and has gotten richer every single one of those years,” Peltola said. Sullivan shot back, referring to a recent New York Times article that described turmoil in her congressional office and campaign, including angry outbursts and offensive language. “Twenty-five staffers quit on Mary Peltola because she abused them physically and emotionally, and then she slanders every other group, African Americans, special needs individuals. It is a character flaw on my opponent,” Sullivan said, referring to the Times’ reporting on her time on Capitol Hill. Peltola was later asked directly about the Times’ reporting. “I don’t think this election is about me on my worst day,” Peltola said, calling the stories “allegations” and “mass exaggerations of the truth.” Thursday’s debate comes just days after Trump visited Wasilla, Alaska, to hold a rally in support of Sullivan amid his multistate blitz to shore up Republican candidates, and Vice President JD Vance visited Fairbanks earlier this month. The subject of Trump, however, was largely absent from Thursday’s debate, a departure from other high-profile races. Alaska last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2008, when Sen. Mark Begich ousted incumbent Republican Ted Stevens. Peltola finished ahead of Sullivan in August’s all-party primary, with Peltola receiving 49.5% of the vote and Sullivan taking 41.4%. A second Republican candidate also named Dan Sullivan — who has denied Republican accusations of being a ploy to confuse voters — received only 2.5% of the vote. Dan J. Sullivan did not participate in Thursday night’s debate, although he will be on the ballot in November.

articles.title: The system failed Jane Doe. Congress can fix it.
articles.summary: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand called for the passage of the Campus Accountability and Safety Act to address systemic failures in protecting students following allegations of sexual assault at Cornell University.
articles.body:
In recent weeks, the horrific allegations of sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house have sparked public outrage.

But as debates about campus culture and law enforcement lapses permeated the public conscience, Congress made clear that it had a very different priority: debating regulations for college sports . Not a second was spent on campus safety at a time that one in four undergraduate women report being sexually assaulted at school. At Cornell, that figure is more than one in three .

There is no question: the system has failed Jane Doe.

This is not just a problem with one case, one fraternity, or one university. Jane Doe’s story echoes a heartbreaking reality on campuses across the country. Time and time again, victims experience the same story: they report, then watch their perpetrators get by with a slap on the wrist.

In 2016 , America watched Stanford swimmer Brock Turner serve just three months in jail for raping an unconscious woman behind a campus dumpster. The survivor’s victim impact statement went viral. Over a million people signed petitions calling for the judge in Turner’s case to be removed. California lawmakers subsequently changed the state’s sentencing laws.

This should have been a turning point. It wasn’t.

In 2016, Baylor also came under fire after an investigation found administrators had discouraged students from reporting sexual assault. In 2021, USC announced it would pay millions to women who said the university ignored years of complaints about sexual abuse by its campus gynecologist. In the years since, dozens of institutions have come under federal investigation over alleged mishandling of Title IX sexual violence cases.

A system that fails survivors repeatedly is fundamentally broken. The price of a college education shouldn’t include a greater than 25 percent chance of being sexually assaulted.

Congress must do more to protect students. We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act .

CASA is commonsense, bipartisan legislation. It would hold institutions accountable, uphold a fair process for students, and give sexual assault survivors a trauma-informed advocate to help them through the adjudication process.

Cornell offers confidential resources for students, and we don’t know the extent to which Jane Doe knew about or used them. But not all universities offer those resources, and even if they do, many students don’t know they exist.

First, it would require a trained, confidential advocate to be available to survivors of sexual assault on every campus.

The trauma of sexual assault can impair memory and make bureaucracy feel impossible. Having an advocate who is trained in trauma-informed care ensures that survivors are not re-traumatized by the very system meant to protect them.

Such an advocate could have been life-changing for someone like Jane Doe.

They could have walked Doe through the complex disciplinary process that comes with reporting an assault. They could have talked her through her options, including the difference between Cornell’s disciplinary process and the criminal process. And when Doe chose to report, they could have acted as her liaison with the university and law enforcement, sparing her the trauma of reliving her experience every time she spoke with a different authority figure.

Crucially, CASA would require campus staff who receive reports of sexual assault and domestic violence — including the Cornell Health medical clinic employee whom Jane Doe saw — to provide those students with contact information for the on-campus advocate and an explanation of the services they offer.

Second, CASA would require uniform, rigorous training for all campus personnel involved in investigating and adjudicating sexual assault cases.

That training could have helped prevent critical errors in Doe’s case.

For example, Doe’s lawyer alleges that the Tompkins County District Attorney never contacted her after she made her initial statement to Cornell police. A New York Times investigation later showed that a key statement from Doe’s testimony — “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped” — was left out of the six-page statement that was sent to the district attorney.

Better-trained investigators are far less likely to make that mistake.

At the same time, a CASA advocate could have helped Doe review her testimony and caught the omission. Then, once the complaint was submitted to the district attorney, they could have helped follow up on her case and demanded that her complaint be taken seriously.

Advocates and training help survivors navigate the system — but that is only half the battle. CASA also fixes the system itself, making it more transparent and fair for all students.

The legislation would mandate a uniform process for conducting campus disciplinary proceedings surrounding sexual assault. That means no separate track for athletes or students in fraternities.

CASA also protects students who come forward by encouraging the adoption of a practical amnesty policy in cases like Jane Doe’s, where alcohol or drugs are involved. CASA would help shield students who report in good faith from being disciplined for drinking or illegal substance use.

And finally, CASA would require colleges and universities to disclose key data about the prevalence of sexual assault on their campuses and the outcomes of sexual assault investigations. Institutions that fail to comply would face financial penalties.

Transparency creates accountability. If students and families can see what is happening on campus, and how universities respond, institutions will finally be incentivized to put safety first.

Passing CASA will not end sexual violence on college campuses, nor will it undo the harm already inflicted on countless survivors. Changing the culture that allows campus sexual assault to persist will require sustained commitment at every level — from universities, students, families, law enforcement, and lawmakers. But establishing a fair process, giving survivors an advocate, and mandating real accountability is an essential start.

The system failed Jane Doe. It has failed too many survivors for too long. Congress can change that. We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act.

Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat, is New York’s junior U.S. senator.

articles.title: Trump's Capitol Hill whisperer reveals secrets to president's dealmaking as he heads for exit
articles.summary: James Braid spoke with Fox News Digital about his work the last two years on his way out of the Trump administration.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: There are few people in the United States who have more significantly shaped the course of American history over the last two years, while remaining as little-known as James Braid. Millions of Americans across the country may not be familiar with the name, but in Washington, D.C., Braid is hard to miss both literally and figuratively. At 6 feet, 6 inches tall, he cast a tall shadow during his days at the White House and on Capitol Hill pushing President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda. And that shadow has been responsible for helping push numerous legislative successes for Trump over the finish line, from rolling back Biden-era policies to passing Trump’s signature tax policy bill, until Tuesday — which marked Braid’s last day as director of the Office of Legislative Affairs. The "stock-in-trade" of the job, he told Fox News Digital in a rare interview, "is cautious optimism in the face of all odds." From the outside, being Trump’s whisperer on Capitol Hill does not look like an easy job, particularly when the president is known to personally call out lawmakers who oppose his agenda. Recently, for example, he publicized the personal phone number of Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., over his opposition to a bill making daylight saving time permanent. TRUMP DROPS REPUBLICAN SENATOR'S PHONE NUMBER IN SOCIAL POST OVER FURY ON STALLED BILL But Braid insisted that Trump’s people skills ultimately meant those dust-ups came out of the wash and lauded "his extraordinary capacity to have a tough conversation one day and play a round of golf the next." "There's always a give-and-take in any relationship with a legislator, and sometimes there's a give as a result of, you know, tension," Braid said. "But you know … one errant Truth [Social post], or one critical Truth, does not a relationship make." But some Republicans’ relationships with the president never seemed to recover, like in the case of Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., who has no love lost with Trump. Braid said the key to working with people was always being straightforward about what the White House wants. "We've been able to be honest brokers and deliver for a lot of these members in different ways," he said. But Trump’s presence still looms large in Congress whether he’s there in person or not. A senior administration official familiar with Braid’s work told Fox News Digital that ultimately, "No one speaks for President Trump except for President Trump." The official said Trump is known to be "hands-on at every critical legislative juncture" that pushes his agenda forward. And Braid revealed that he keeps tabs on certain votes, as well. "He always wants to know how people are voting after every major vote. He knows where people are," Braid said, adding that Trump "ultimately knows that Republicans in Congress overwhelmingly vote with him." But Braid admitted he has faced long odds over his last two years, particularly with the vast tax-and-policy package nicknamed the Big, Beautiful Bill. MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400 He recalled sitting in his office one day, "I looked at the quad on the TV, and every single chyron is some variation of ‘GOP megabill in trouble.’ And yeah, I mean, there's certainly, at every moment, it was tenuous. At every moment, the thread was fraying." One specific scenario he recalled took place at Sterling Golf Club in Virginia, where he, Trump, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought and then-deputy chief of staff James Blair were meeting with Senate Republican holdouts on the legislation. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' "We're sitting there with [Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.], [Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.], [Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla.], me, Blair, Russ and the president, and they're bringing out these heaps of food," Braid recalled. "I think there's something like four pizzas on the table and maybe 22 hot dogs for five guys, none of them were eating. And it's just, I mean, we, I think we argued about the administration's overall funding strategy for two hours as the afternoon wore on." Ultimately, however, the bill passed the House and Senate — for which Braid credited both administration officials and congressional leaders. "The level of commitment that was there and present from the leadership across the Republican Party to get this thing done, basically willed it into being," he said. He referenced the day Trump signed the bill when asked about his best day on the job over the last two years: "I would say July 4th in the White House with my son and the speaker of the House in the summer sunshine, watching the president sign the most significant piece of Republican domestic policy legislation." Top congressional leaders hailed Braid as a critical champion of the GOP agenda. "James is a total pro and one of House Republicans’ greatest teammates," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said. "He took the time to get to know our members and master the unique dynamics of the House Republican Conference." Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called Braid a "tremendous partner" for his conference. "I’m grateful for his dedicated service to our country, and I wish him and his family all the best with their next chapter," Thune said. Vought called Braid a "lion for the president in delivering his agenda on the Hill." And Vice President JD Vance, who hired Braid as his legislative director before both ascended to the White House, told Fox News Digital that he is "incredibly brilliant, effective and a hard worker without compare." "He has been with me since the start of my Senate term, where he was with me for every fight and brought his talents to the president’s second term, where he has played a central role in every single policy effort since," Vance said. Now that he is departing, the senior administration official who spoke with Fox News Digital said they expect Braid to find work outside the government after years of grinding on Capitol Hill and the White House. As for Braid, he said of his next move, "It's hard for me to even think about not doing this job, but at the end of the day, I know [Katie Bailey is] going to do great … but yeah, I'll take a little time and try to figure out what's next." Bailey, Braid's former deputy director of the Office of Legislative Affairs, is now taking over the job. He summed up his advice to his successor in two bullet points. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Number one, you have to be ruthless in what you're focused on and tune out the distractions to get the issue of the day over the line and onto the president's desk," he said. "Number two, invariably, the situation feels pretty grave, but usually we muddle through, and to remain optimistic."

articles.title: Democrats call for gun control after Oregon school shooter reportedly uses shotgun purchased by his mother
articles.summary: A 16-year-old gunman broke into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three children and a teacher before an armed bystander intervened.
articles.body: Several high-profile Democratic lawmakers renewed calls for gun control after a teenager broke into an Oregon elementary school Thursday and fatally shot three children and a teacher before being killed by an armed bystander. Sen. Ron Wyden, who has represented Oregon in the Senate since 1996, made one of the most explicit calls for tighter gun laws following the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where the 16-year-old attacker used his mother’s shotgun, according to The Associated Press. "The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass common-sense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Ore., said Thursday night that "the epidemic of gun violence in schools across America must come to an end." GEORGIA HIGH SCHOOL SHOOTING SUSPECT COLT GRAY CHANGES PLEA TO GUILTY, NOW FACES LIFE IN PRISON "No parent should have to wonder if their child will come home at the end of the day," Bonamici said. "Children deserve to feel safe — and be safe — in school." Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum represents Oregon’s 5th Congressional District, which includes Bend. She attended a nighttime vigil for the teacher and children — aged 5, 8 and 11 — who were killed in the shooting. "When are we going to step up and say enough of killing our babies? When are we going to say that we need safe schools, that we need to make sure that people who should not have firearms don’t have them? When are we going to stop making excuses? When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?" Bynum told KTVZ 21, a local NBC station in Bend, at the event. Statements from Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and the state's Democratic governor, Tina Kotek, stopped short of calling for new regulation on guns, but both made it clear gun violence should have no place in American schools. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS Democrats outside of Oregon appeared a bit freer to express support for going further on gun control, especially in the early aftermath of the shooting, which also left another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, critically injured. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., said the gun reforms Congress passed after the Uvalde school shooting — including enhanced background checks for buyers under 21 — did not go far enough. "Much more must be done. Not a single child should be lost to gun violence. Ever," Heinrich said in a statement posted to social media. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who supports federal red-flag laws and universal background checks, had a similar message. "No family should ever have to suffer like this—and there have been over 50 school shootings just this year," she wrote on social media. "Congress must do much more to prevent gun violence." DOJ TARGETS SPANBERGER, NEWSOM GUN LAWS WITH TWIN LAWSUITS AFTER SCOTUS AFFIRMS SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS The reactions from lawmakers came as authorities in Bend continue to piece together how the deadly attack unfolded and how the teenage gunman obtained the weapon he used. Police said they did not know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended when he was younger. The first emergency call came at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone carrying a long gun, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Thursday. Dispatchers then received dozens of calls reporting that a shooter had entered the school. Officers arrived within three minutes of the first emergency call. Moments later, an officer reported that a "community member" had shot the teenage suspect. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Silver Rail Elementary School, which is about 125 miles southeast of Portland, has a total of 467 students this academic year. It serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade. After the shooting, students were bused to a nearby church that served as a family reunification center, where relieved parents embraced their children and walked them to their cars, some carrying stuffed animals and other comfort items they had brought from home, The Associated Press reported. The Bend-La Pine school district canceled classes, sporting events and extracurricular activities Friday across all 32 of its schools. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
